  Earnings data collection practices

 Introduction
Current international statistical standards on income generated through employment are contained in the
Resolution concerning the measurement of employment-related income adopted by the 16th International Conference
of Labour Statisticians (ICLS) in 1998 and updated at the 21st ICLS in 2023.
The resolution establishes a comprehensive framework for measuring the remuneration derived from
employment activities by both independent and dependent workers.
It also makes recommendations on sources to collect data on the topic, classifying them, at general level, into two
groups based on the nature of reporting units – households or establishments.
This report presents the results of a survey on practices of data collection of employee income from
establishments, that is, it does not cover practices related to data collection in household surveys and those
related to measuring profit derived from independent (self-employment) activities.
The survey was conducted between November 2025 and March 2026 aiming to update the existing knowledge
and support national implementation of standards. It collected key information about national administrative
sources, economic censuses or surveys used by official statistics to collect earnings data from establishments.

3

  Earnings data collection practices

 Survey methodology
The online questionnaire was developed in Excel Forms and an invitation to participate in the survey containing
the link1 was sent to known email addresses of national statistical agencies.
Initial invitations to participate in the survey were sent on the 21st of November. By the end of January 2026, 53
countries had participated providing information on a total number of 99 data sources, or on plans to collect
earnings data in the future. To increase the sample and improve geographical coverage, a reminder was sent to
countries which hadn’t participated and ILO regional statisticians made efforts to motivate countries. As a result,
by the end of March, a total number of 81 countries 2, representing almost 60% of the global population, had
provided data.
The questionnaire was designed to collect detailed information on any source used to collect data from 2020 to
2025 to produce official statistics of employee earnings. For countries which hadn’t collected earnings data during
that period, questions were designed to request summary information on possible data collection before 2020
and on any plans to do so in the future.
Dedicated questions were designed to collect the following information about data sources:
● Type (census, administrative source, survey)
● Key sample design characteristics for surveys (stratification, sample selection and size)
● Data collection frequency, mode and reference period
● Geographical coverage
● Coverage of economic activities
● Type of units providing data (size, head/local unit, profit/non-profit, ownership,
incorporated/unincorporated)
● Type of employee collected (individual/aggregated, types of employees, employee characteristics, number
of persons / full-time equivalents, average/stock numbers)
● Type of data on hours worked collected
● Earnings components on which data are collected
The analysis of this information allowed producing a detailed picture of national approaches to collecting
earnings data from establishments.

  Earnings data collection practices

 Survey results

Data sources
Countries generally rely on multiple complementary sources to produce earnings statistics, with sample
surveys being the most common, followed by administrative sources and economic censuses. This diversity
reflects different statistical objectives and institutional arrangements. Administrative sources have become a
key component of national earnings statistics where suitable registers exist, while surveys remain
indispensable for collecting variables not available in administrative records.
Of the 81 countries which participated in the survey, 68 had collected official earnings data between 2020 and
2025 and had provided information on 136 data sources (an average of 2 sources per country and a maximum of
8).
Most participating countries are from Europe3 (41%), representing 74% of the region’s population. The second
most represented region is Americas – while participating countries represent only 20% of the total number, the
region’s population coverage reached the highest level (87%).
Similar shares of countries form Asia and the Pacific and from Africa participated in the survey, however,
population coverage was lower – 53% and 35% respectively.
Only four Arab States participated, but covering 41% of the region’s population aged 15 years and over.

Five countries provided information on household surveys (mainly Labour Force Survey) used to collect earnings
data. While such sources were not in the scope of the survey, it is important to note that in some countries they
could be the only source of earnings data covering most or all employees (mainly where informal employment
rates are very high). A dedicated report describing earnings data collection practices in Labour Force Surveys will
be produced later.
This report focuses on practices applied in collecting data from establishments only, therefore, the five cases were
excluded from the analysis presented further, which is based on 131 sources reported by 66 countries.

Data collection frequency, mode, and response rates
Most establishment sources operate on a regular schedule, predominantly annually, providing a stable basis
for producing official earnings statistics. Administrative sources stand out for their high collection frequency
and extremely high comprehensiveness for the population covered, while surveys and censuses rely more
heavily on mixed collection approaches combining self-reporting with interviewer support. The widespread use
of self-administered reporting may indicate continuing digitalization of data collection, although regional
differences suggest interviewer-assisted collection remains important in certain statistical systems.

Data collection frequency
Of the 131 sources collecting data from establishments, most (126) do so regularly – every year (79%), every two
years (6%), every four years (9%)5 and every five years (6%).
All reported surveys are conducted regularly, with a predefined frequency. The 9 cases of sources used to collect
data irregularly were administrative sources (6) and economic censuses (3). The highest share of irregular sources
was reported by countries from Americas (15%).
Unsurprisingly, due to low data collection costs, administrative sources are those used most frequently – almost
all of them (97%) are used each year. Surveys, which usually collect most complex/rich data, follow next with 73%
of them being used each year. Economic censuses, requiring full coverage of establishments and collection of
great quantities of data, are the sources used least frequently.

All cases refer to the Structure of earnings survey conducted in EU countries, candidate countries, and European Free Trade Association (EFTA)
countries every four years.

Shares of sources collecting data each year are higher in Americas, Europe and Arab States (over 75%), and lower
in Africa, Asia and Pacific (64%). In terms of countries, if sources of all types are considered then over 86% of
countries collect data each year.

Data collection mode
In most sources (71%), data are collected through self-reporting which means asking establishments to fill in and
deliver (electronic or paper) forms using guidance provided by statistical authorities. About a fifth (22%) of
sources apply a mixed approach combining self-reporting with data collection by interviewers and only 7% collect
all data through interviews.
As expected, administrative sources rely almost exclusively on self-reporting (95%), with very limited involvement
of interviewers – 5% apply the mixed approach. Economic censuses and sample surveys apply self-reporting less
frequently (60 to 65%) and rely more on the mixed approach (about 30%). Data collection only by interviewers is
practiced in 4% of administrative sources and 11% of sample surveys.
Reliance on self-reporting is the highest in Europe (91%) and lowest in Africa and Arab States (about 30%), where
a significant share of data are collected by interviewers.

Response rate
The overall response rate across all sources is 86%, with the highest value (96%) for administrative resources and
lower values (about 82%) for economic censuses and sample surveys.

Sample surveys
Establishment surveys show a high degree of methodological consistency. Stratification by economic activity
and establishment size has become standard practice, often supplemented by geographical location. Many
countries combine probability sampling with certainty selection of economically important establishments,
balancing statistical efficiency with the need to accurately measure large employers that account for a
substantial share of employment and earnings.

Stratification
Of the 70 establishment surveys reported, 66 use stratification when extracting the sample. Most frequently used
stratification variables, applied in over 85% of surveys, are economic activity and establishment size (number of
employees). In 80% of surveys, these variables are used simultaneously.

Other characteristics used for stratification less frequently are location 6 (55%), ownership type (21%),
revenue/profit value (20%) and others (14%).
Most frequently (46%), three variables are used to stratify the sample frame, combined use of economic activity,
establishment size and location being the preferred option.
Use of two stratification variables is the second most common approach (29%). In most cases economic activity
and establishment size are used.
Ownership type, revenue/profit value and other characteristics are in almost all cases used for stratification as
additional variables.

Sample selection
For half of the surveys, the sample is selected applying a mixed approach – some units are selected randomly and
some non-randomly. This practice is predominant in Americas (71%). Almost in all cases, the non-random
component of the sample represents a census of units considered important, influencing significantly
employment and the national economy in general. Such units are allocated to special strata using one or several
criteria – establishment size being the most frequently applied. Other common criteria are the type of economic
activity and revenue/profit value. Capital size and foreign control are used less frequently. In half cases, a
combination of two or three criteria is used to identify units assigned to the census strata.
Where the non-random survey component is not a census, it is a sub-sample designed to observe the most
important part – for example, the group of establishments with highest revenue holding 80% of total value. Such
groups are also maintained as longitudinal panels.
Only random selection is applied in about 39% of surveys samples. This approach is predominant in Europe (49%).
The practice of using only non-random samples is very limited (7%) and consists in observing the most important
establishments (mainly in terms of revenue value).

Reference period
Monthly (43%) and annual (39%) reference periods dominate earnings data collection, reflecting the different
purposes served by administrative systems, surveys and censuses. Quarterly and weekly reference periods are
rarely used.
Administrative sources are primarily designed around regular payroll reporting and therefore favour monthly
observation (71%), whereas annual reference periods are more commonly used in economic censuses and
surveys where broader structural information is collected. This diversity highlights the need to consider reference
periods carefully when comparing or integrating data across sources.

The preferred reference period in Europe and Africa is the month (around 50%), while in other regions it’s the year
(about 55%).

Coverage of economic activities
Although most sources cover all economic activities, comprehensive coverage is not yet universal. A substantial
number of data collections are either sector-specific or intentionally exclude selected activities for which
alternative data sources exist. Consequently, users should account for differences in industry coverage when
interpreting national earnings statistics or undertaking international comparisons.
Only 61% of sources collect data from establishments operating in all economic activities 7. Administrative sources
do so in almost all cases (95%), economic censuses in over half of cases (57%) and sample surveys less frequently
(44%).
Cases where not all activities are covered can be classified into two groups:
● Sources designed to collect data only from specific sectors – only one or few activities covered (for
example, financial sector, industry, trade, public sector). They represent about 20% of all sources.
● Sources excluding one or few activities (like agriculture, public administration, education,
financial/insurance activity) for which more appropriate sources exist or are specially designed.
Sources in Africa and Europe cover all economic activities more frequently (73%) than in the rest of the world
(45%).
During data collection, 63% of sources ask establishments to provide data only on their main activity – the one
which contributes most to the unit’s total output (value added, revenue or production). In very rare cases, sources
identify the main activity based on the highest labour input (number of employees).

  Earnings data collection practices

Coverage of reporting units
The survey indicates that most establishment-based earnings collections aim for broad institutional coverage,
including public and private sectors as well as various legal forms of enterprises. Nevertheless, differences
remain regarding the treatment of small establishments, unincorporated units, foreign-owned enterprises,
cooperatives and non-profit organizations. These differences can influence both the representativeness and
comparability of resulting earnings indicators.
Most data sources (71%) do not use the number of employees as a criterion to exclude units from data collection.
However, those that do so use a threshold of 10 employees or less in most cases and apply it (with very few
exceptions) across all economic activities.
When applying this threshold, most sources (74%) consider all types of employees working at the unit and fewer
(26%) target specific groups like full-time/regular employees, those with direct contracts.
Data from both private and public establishments are collected by most sources (85%). About 12% of sources limit
data collection to private units and very few (2%) to public ones.
Only 8% of sources exclude units owned (totally or partially) by foreign entities. In most cases, these are sources
collecting data from unincorporated or public units.
Unincorporated units are covered by 63% of sources, coverage being higher for administrative sources and
economic censuses (79%) compared to sample surveys (50%).
Most sources collect data from cooperatives (80%) and non-profit organizations (73%), coverage being higher for
administrative sources (87%) and economic censuses (74%).

Treatment of sub-units
Countries are almost evenly divided between collecting information directly from local establishments and
obtaining consolidated data from enterprise headquarters. In a few cases, sample surveys do not collect any
information on sub-units. This reflects different statistical unit concepts and administrative practices. The choice
affects the geographical and industrial detail that can be produced and should therefore be considered when
designing establishment-based earnings statistics.
Economic surveys tend to treat sub-units as independent data providers to a larger degree than other sources
(65% against 45%). Same approach seems to be applied to sources in Americas, Assia and the Pacific compared to
other regions.

Type of data collected
Most sources collect information covering all employees, although significant differences exist in the level of
detail. Administrative sources primarily collect individual-level records, while surveys and especially economic
censuses more often collect aggregated information. Where individual records are collected, employee
characteristics such as sex, age, occupation and job type (full/part-time) are widely available, enabling detailed
analysis of earnings differentials. Aggregated collections remain focused mainly on totals, with more limited
disaggregation by employee characteristics.
Collecting data on all employees working for economic units is the predominant practice (92%). Requesting data
only on specific groups (full-time/permanent employees, specific occupations) is an approach rarely applied.
Most sources collect aggregated employee data (59%), economic censuses doing so at the highest rate (91%),
followed by sample surveys (64%). Administrative sources, on the other hand, collect mostly individual employee
data (71%).
Europe seems to be the region with the highest share of sources collecting individual data (51%) and Africa and
Americas with the lowest (about 28%).
10

  Earnings data collection practices

Individual data
In all administrative sources and economic censuses, units provide individual data on all their employees (unitlevel census). Only 42% of sample surveys follow this practice, in 27% cases units provide data samples of
employees while 31% of surveys combine unit-level census and sampling.
Almost all sources (96%) collect data on employee characteristics. The most frequently collected being sex (82%),
full/part-time (695), age (67%) and occupation (65%). Other characteristics, like education level and job tenure, are
collected less frequently. None of the reported sources collects data that could provide information on the
employees’ family – like marital status, household size, number of children, etc.

Aggregated data
Sources collecting aggregated data mostly (87%) ask units to provide the total value of indicators (e.g. employees,
remuneration, hours worked). Only few sources ask for average values (5%) or both totals and averages (8%).
About 66% of sources ask units to provide aggregated data by employee characteristics. Sex (53%), full/part-time
(33%) and occupation (18%) being the most frequently collected variables.

Employment and working-time measures
Data on the number of employees
Most sources collect employee counts, while information on full-time equivalents is considerably less common.
Collection of hours worked is widespread but not universal, with surveys more frequently capturing this
information than administrative sources. Differences in whether sources measure hours worked, hours paid,
overtime or contractual hours underline the importance of precise metadata when interpreting earnings
measures, particularly those expressed on an hourly basis.
By default, in sources collecting individual data units provide the number of persons employed by unit, which
then can be used to calculate full-time equivalents (FTE). Sources collecting aggregated data, on the other hand,
must choose what data to request. Most of them (65%) request units to report numbers of employees, few (9%)
request FTEs and one quarter (26%) ask for both indicators.
Whether sources collect aggregated numbers of employees or FTEs, there are two main approaches in relation to
the moment these numbers refer to:
● At the beginning or end of the reference period, applied in 40% of sources
● Average number for the reference period, applied in 43% of sources
About 17% of sources apply both approaches.

Data on hours worked
Almost two-thirds (63%) of sources collect data on hours worked. Sample surveys do so more frequently (75%),
compared to economic censuses (58%) and administrative sources (45%). Collection of data on hours worked has
higher prevalence in Europe (77%) compared to other regions (46%).
Data on hours worked and paid are collected by most sources (82%), regardless of their type. Other types of
working hours often considered are overtime (63%) and normal/contractual hours (54%). Fewer sources collect
data on hours worked and not paid (15%) or on hours not worked but paid (22%).
Few sources (mainly surveys) collect data on all these five types of hours. On average, a source collects data on
two types.

11

  Earnings data collection practices

Earnings data
While cash remuneration is collected universally, countries vary considerably in the range of additional
earnings components measured. Bonuses and gratuities are widely covered, whereas remuneration for time
not worked, payments in kind, housing allowances, overtime pay and unpaid wages are collected less
consistently. These differences affect the extent to which national statistics align with the comprehensive
concept of employment-related income defined in international standards and should be considered in
international comparisons.
Bonuses and gratuities are the earnings component measured by most sources (81%), especially in Europe (95%)
and Asia and Pacific (80%). The usual practice is to collect data on all bonuses and gratuities (88%) not only on
those paid regularly (12%). Bonuses covered are year-end and seasonal bonuses (93%), profit-sharing bonuses
(82%), supplementary vacation and other bonuses (88%).
Remuneration for time not worked is the second component frequently measured with 62% of sources collecting
data, with highest rate in Europe (71%). All sources covering this component collect data on payments related to
paid leaves. Almost all cover payments for public and other holidays (91%) and other types of time off granted
with pay (85%).
Payments in kind are covered by half of sources with highest prevalence among economic censuses and surveys
in Europe (63%).
Fewer sources collect data on housing and rental allowances (39%) and on overtime remuneration (37%); and very
few on unpaid wages/salaries.

Data collection plans
The survey also indicates positive prospects for expanding establishment-based earnings statistics. Of the 13
countries that did not collect earnings data during the reference period, 10 reported plans to introduce new data
collections between 2026 and 2029. Four of them indicated household surveys as sources of data.
This suggests continued progress towards improved availability of official earnings statistics, although household
surveys will remain an important complementary source in countries where establishment-based systems are still
under development.
